# Three-Dimensional Amplitude Measurements in B → ψ(2S)K* and B → χc1K* Decays

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of exclusive B meson decays to charmonium states and vector kaon resonances (K*) provides a rich laboratory for testing the predictions of the Standard Model and probing the underlying dynamics of heavy quark decay. Among these processes, the decays B→ψ(2S)K* and B→χc1K* have historically received less experimental attention than the well-studied B→J/ψK* channel, primarily due to their lower branching fractions and the experimental challenges associated with reconstructing their final states. This work addresses this gap by presenting, for the first time, a complete three-dimensional measurement of the decay amplitudes governing B→ψ(2S)K* and B→χc1K* transitions. In parallel, we provide a refined and updated analysis of the B→J/ψK* decay, incorporating improved statistical precision and methodological consistency, thereby enabling a direct and meaningful comparison across all three charmonium-K* decay modes.

## Experimental Setup and Data Sample

The analysis is based on data collected with the BaBar detector operating at the PEP-II asymmetric-energy e+e− storage ring located at SLAC. The dataset comprises an extensive sample corresponding to 232 million BB̄ pairs, produced via the Υ(4S) resonance. This substantial statistical sample represents one of the largest available datasets for B meson physics at the time of this study, providing the necessary sensitivity to perform a full angular analysis of the three decay modes under consideration. The large sample size is particularly crucial for the χc1K* and ψ(2S)K* channels, which suffer from smaller branching fractions and more challenging reconstruction efficiencies compared to the J/ψK* mode.

The three-dimensional amplitude analysis employed in this study allows for the complete characterization of the decay dynamics by disentangling the various helicity amplitudes contributing to each process. This approach provides access not only to the magnitudes of the longitudinal and transverse polarization amplitudes but also to their relative phases, offering a comprehensive picture of the decay mechanism that goes beyond simpler branching fraction measurements.

## Polarization Structure and Charmonium Quantum Numbers

One of the central findings of this analysis concerns the polarization structure of the three decay modes, which is intimately connected to the quantum numbers of the charmonium state involved. The results demonstrate a clear and systematic difference in the longitudinal polarization fraction depending on whether the charmonium state possesses J^PC=1^−− quantum numbers (as is the case for both J/ψ and ψ(2S)) or J^PC=1^++ quantum numbers (characteristic of χc1).

Specifically, the measurements reveal that the longitudinal polarization fraction is significantly enhanced in the B→χc1K* decay relative to both B→J/ψK* and B→ψ(2S)K*. This observation is particularly interesting from a theoretical standpoint, as it suggests that the underlying decay dynamics—governed by the interplay of strong and weak interaction effects—are sensitive to the C-parity and parity quantum numbers of the charmonium state. Such a distinction provides valuable input for theoretical models attempting to describe the factorization properties and helicity amplitude hierarchies in B meson decays to charmonium and light vector mesons. The consistency of this pattern across the χc1 channel, in contrast to the two vector charmonium states, strengthens the interpretation that the quantum number assignment plays a decisive role in shaping the polarization landscape of these decays.

## Search for CP Violation

In addition to the polarization measurements, this analysis includes a dedicated search for direct CP violation in the form of charge asymmetries across all three decay channels. Direct CP violation, if observed, would manifest as a measurable difference between the decay rates of B mesons and their charge-conjugate B̄ meson counterparts, providing insight into the interplay of weak phases and strong final-state interactions within these decay processes.

The results of this search show no statistically significant evidence for direct CP-violating charge asymmetries in any of the three measured decays: B→J/ψK*, B→ψ(2S)K*, and B→χc1K*. This null result is consistent with Standard Model expectations, given that these decays are dominated by a single weak amplitude (or amplitudes with negligible relative weak phase), which typically suppresses the generation of observable direct CP asymmetries. Nonetheless, the absence of such asymmetries within the current experimental precision serves as an important consistency check and provides a benchmark against which future, more precise measurements—potentially sensitive to smaller CP-violating effects—can be compared.

## Conclusion

This study represents a significant advancement in the experimental characterization of B meson decays to charmonium and K* final states. By providing the first three-dimensional amplitude measurements for B→ψ(2S)K* and B→χc1K*, alongside an updated and consistent treatment of B→J/ψK*, this work offers a comprehensive comparative framework for understanding the polarization structure of these decays. The observed enhancement of longitudinal polarization in the χc1 channel relative to the J/ψ and ψ(2S) channels highlights the important role of charmonium quantum numbers in shaping decay dynamics, while the absence of direct CP violation across all three modes is consistent with theoretical expectations within the Standard Model. These results, enabled by the large BaBar dataset of 232 million BB̄ pairs, contribute valuable experimental constraints for ongoing theoretical efforts to model exclusive B decays to charmonium states.

# Three-Dimensional Angular Analysis of B → ψ(2S)K*, B → χc1K*, and B → J/ψK* Decays

## I. Introduction

The study of exclusive B meson decays to charmonium states plus a K* meson provides a rich laboratory for testing our understanding of both the weak and strong interactions. These decays, mediated by the color-suppressed tree diagram b → c c̄ s, proceed through three helicity amplitudes when the charmonium state has spin greater than zero and the K* is reconstructed in a vector final state such as K*⁰ → K⁺π⁻. The relative magnitudes and phases of these amplitudes encode information about the underlying dynamics of hadronization and provide sensitive probes of factorization-based predictions, final-state interactions, and potential new physics contributions that could manifest as anomalous strong phases or unexpected polarization patterns.

The decay B → J/ψK* has been extensively studied by several experiments and serves as the benchmark channel for this class of measurements. In contrast, the decays B → ψ(2S)K* and B → χc1K* have received comparatively little experimental attention due to their smaller branching fractions and the more challenging reconstruction of the ψ(2S) and χc1 charmonium states. A complete three-dimensional angular analysis of all three channels, performed with consistent methodology and using a single dataset, allows for a direct comparison of the polarization structure across final states involving charmonium mesons of different quantum numbers: the 1⁻⁻ J/ψ and ψ(2S) vector states, and the 1⁺⁺ χc1 axial-vector state.

Naive factorization arguments and heavy-quark symmetry considerations lead to specific expectations for the relative size of the longitudinal and transverse polarization amplitudes in these decays. In particular, models based on factorization predict a dominant longitudinal polarization amplitude for B → J/ψK*, in qualitative but not quantitative agreement with previous measurements, which found significant transverse polarization contributions inconsistent with naive expectations. It is of interest to determine whether the χc1K* mode, which involves a charmonium state of different parity and quantum numbers, exhibits similar patterns or is dominated by longitudinal polarization in a manner more consistent with theoretical expectations. Furthermore, any observation of direct CP violation, manifested as an asymmetry in the decay rates or in the interference terms between B⁰ and B̄⁰ decays, would provide crucial information given that these decays are theoretically expected to be essentially free of significant CP violation within the Standard Model, making them useful control channels for CP violation searches in related modes.

## II. The BaBar Detector and Dataset

This analysis is based on a data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity containing approximately 232 million BB̄ pairs, collected with the BaBar detector operating at the PEP-II asymmetric-energy e⁺e⁻ storage ring at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The data were recorded at the Υ(4S) resonance, with the center-of-mass energy tuned to produce B⁰B̄⁰ and B⁺B⁻ pairs nearly at rest in the Υ(4S) rest frame.

The BaBar detector is a general-purpose spectrometer described in detail elsewhere. Charged particle tracking is provided by a five-layer silicon vertex tracker (SVT) and a 40-layer drift chamber (DCH) operating within a 1.5 T solenoidal magnetic field. Charged hadron identification is achieved through measurements of ionization energy loss (dE/dx) in the tracking devices combined with information from a detector of internally reflected Cherenkov light (DIRC). Photon and electron energies are measured with a CsI(Tl) electromagnetic calorimeter (EMC), while muon identification is provided by the instrumented flux return (IFR) located outside of the magnet coil.

## III. Event Reconstruction and Selection

Candidates for the charmonium states are reconstructed in several decay modes. The J/ψ and ψ(2S) mesons are reconstructed through their leptonic decays to e⁺e⁻ and μ⁺μ⁻ pairs, with bremsstrahlung recovery applied for electron candidates to improve the invariant mass resolution. Additionally, the ψ(2S) meson is reconstructed via its decay to J/ψπ⁺π⁻, where the J/ψ subsequently decays leptonically. The χc1 meson is reconstructed via its radiative decay to J/ψγ.

The K* meson is reconstructed in the K⁺π⁻ final state (and its charge conjugate), with the invariant mass required to be consistent with the nominal K*(892) mass within a window determined by studies of signal Monte Carlo simulation. Charged kaon candidates are required to satisfy kaon identification criteria based on the DIRC Cherenkov angle and dE/dx measurements to suppress pion backgrounds.

B meson candidates are formed by combining a charmonium candidate with a K* candidate. Two kinematic variables are used to identify signal B decays and reject combinatorial background: the beam-energy-substituted mass mES = √[(s/2 + p⃗i·p⃗B)²/Ei² − p⃗B²], and the energy difference ΔE = EB − √s/2, where the beam four-momentum (Ei, p⃗i) and the B meson candidate four-momentum (EB, p⃗B) are evaluated in the laboratory frame and s is the square of the center-of-mass energy. Signal events are expected to peak at mES near the nominal B meson mass and at ΔE near zero.

Backgrounds arise primarily from combinatorial combinations in generic BB̄ events and, to a lesser extent, from continuum e⁺e⁻ → qq̄ events. Continuum background is suppressed using event-shape variables that exploit the more jet-like topology of continuum events compared to the more spherical topology of BB̄ events.

## IV. Angular Analysis Formalism

The decay B → (charmonium)K*, followed by K* → Kπ and the leptonic or hadronic decay of the charmonium state, is described by three angles that fully characterize the decay kinematics in the absence of additional structure in the K* system: the angle θtr between the charmonium meson momentum and the normal to the K* decay plane in the B rest frame (the transversity angle), the angle θK between the kaon momentum and the direction opposite the B meson in the K* rest frame, and the angle φtr between the charmonium and K* decay planes.

The differential decay rate can be written as a function of these three angles in terms of three complex transversity amplitudes: A0, the longitudinal amplitude, and A∥ and A⊥, the parallel and perpendicular transverse amplitudes, respectively. For the χc1K* final state, in which the charmonium state has J^PC = 1⁺⁺ rather than 1⁻⁻, the same transversity amplitude formalism applies with an appropriate substitution of angular functions to reflect the different intrinsic parity of the χc1 state relative to the J/ψ and ψ(2S).

The decay rate is expressed as a sum of bilinear combinations of the amplitudes multiplied by known angular functions, with interference terms sensitive to the relative phases between amplitudes. By convention, the amplitude normalization satisfies |A0|² + |A∥|² + |A⊥|² = 1, so that |A0|² represents the fraction of longitudinal polarization, and the phases δ∥ = arg(A∥/A0) and δ⊥ = arg(A⊥/A0) determine the relative strong phases between the amplitudes.

An extended unbinned maximum likelihood fit is performed simultaneously to the reconstructed B candidate invariant mass distributions and the three transversity angles to extract the amplitude magnitudes and phases for each of the three decay modes. The signal probability density function includes the full angular correlation structure predicted by the transversity formalism, convolved with the detector acceptance determined from detailed Monte Carlo simulation. Background contributions are modeled using sideband data control samples and modeled separately in mES, ΔE, and the angular variables.

## V. Results

The fit yields the longitudinal polarization fractions, |A0|², along with the relative phases and magnitudes of the transverse amplitudes, for each of the three decay channels. The measurements confirm previous observations for B → J/ψK*, finding a longitudinal polarization fraction of approximately 60%, with a sizable transverse component and a non-trivial relative phase between the perpendicular and longitudinal amplitudes, indicating the presence of significant final-state interaction effects beyond naive factorization expectations.

For B → ψ(2S)K*, the measured polarization fractions and phases are found to be consistent, within experimental uncertainties, with those measured in the J/ψK* channel, supporting the expectation that the underlying dynamics governing the polarization structure are similar for the two 1⁻⁻ charmonium states, as would be expected if the amplitudes are dominated by short-distance physics common to both modes.

In marked contrast, the B → χc1K* channel exhibits a substantially larger longitudinal polarization fraction, with |A0|² measured to be significantly greater than the values obtained for the vector charmonium modes. This enhanced longitudinal polarization is consistent with expectations based on the different quantum numbers of the χc1 meson and suggests that the transverse amplitude contributions, which are prominent in the J/ψ and ψ(2S) channels, are substantially suppressed when the charmonium state has 1⁺⁺ quantum numbers.

The relative phases measured in the χc1K* channel are also found to differ from those observed in the J/ψK* and ψ(2S)K* channels, providing additional evidence that the strong dynamics governing the transverse and longitudinal amplitude interplay depend sensitively on the parity of the charmonium state involved.

## VI. Search for CP Violation

Using the full angular information, the analysis additionally searches for direct CP violation by comparing the amplitude parameters extracted separately for B⁰ and B̄⁰ decays (and, where applicable, B⁺ and B⁻ decays). No significant difference is observed between the polarization fractions or the relative phases measured for B and B̄ decays in any of the three channels studied. Charge asymmetries in the partial decay rates are similarly found to be consistent with zero within the statistical precision of the sample, with no evidence for an asymmetry exceeding the level expected from Standard Model predictions, which anticipate negligible direct CP violation in these color-suppressed b → cc̄s transitions.

# BABAR: Probing the Universe's Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry

The BaBar experiment stands as one of the most significant particle physics collaborations in modern experimental physics, operating at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in California from 1999 to 2008. Named after the B and B-bar mesons (particles and their antiparticles) it was designed to study, BaBar represented a major international effort involving hundreds of physicists from institutions across the globe.

## The Scientific Mission

The primary goal of BaBar was to investigate a phenomenon known as CP violation—a subtle difference in the behavior of matter and antimatter. This asymmetry is crucial to understanding one of the deepest mysteries in cosmology: why the universe appears to be composed almost entirely of matter, despite the Big Bang theoretically having produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter.

BaBar utilized the PEP-II accelerator, a particle collider that smashed together electrons and positrons at nearly the speed of light. These collisions produced B mesons and their antimatter counterparts, which the detector then meticulously tracked and analyzed.

## Key Discoveries and Contributions

The experiment achieved remarkable success in confirming and measuring CP violation in the B meson system, providing strong experimental support for the Kobayashi-Maskawa mechanism within the Standard Model of particle physics. This work was so significant that it contributed to the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa.

Beyond CP violation studies, BaBar's detector system—featuring sophisticated tracking chambers, calorimeters, and particle identification systems—enabled researchers to explore rare decay processes, search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, and study the properties of tau leptons and charm quarks.

## Legacy

Although BaBar ceased data collection in 2008, the collaboration continued analyzing its vast dataset for years afterward, publishing numerous influential papers. The experiment's findings have profoundly shaped our understanding of fundamental particle physics and continue to inform theoretical models today. BaBar, alongside its Japanese counterpart Belle, established a new standard for precision measurements in flavor physics, leaving a lasting legacy in the field of experimental particle physics.

We further search for evidence of CP violation by comparing the amplitude parameters extracted separately for $B^0$ and $\bar{B}^0$ decays, and discuss the implications of our measurements for the interpretation of related $B \to VV$ decay modes relevant to the extraction of CKM phase information. Systematic uncertainties associated with detector acceptance, background modeling, and interference effects are evaluated in detail.
